findings.forcedInvention: What value a non-monetary act carries against the USD 1,000 per-act ceiling — i.e. whether a confirmed permanent band member can unilaterally remove another member, change their mandate, or authorise a release, or whether those escalate.
findings.claim: The ratified peer seed caps seeded authority at 'USD 1,000 per act' and simultaneously grants seven activities of which at least `administer` and `release` carry no monetary value, so the ceiling is unsatisfiable for them. Three user-facing copy strings in three files take opposite positions on whether `administer` sits under the ceiling, and 01.04.01 D-05 makes agreement between two of them a hard requirement.
findings.evidence: 01.03.03-mandate-scope-delegated-authority.md:41 — '| **Value ceiling** (D-08) | Seeded authority is capped at **USD 1,000 per act**, configurable per band. Acts above the ceiling escalate to the owning-mandate holder, who is uncapped | Band orgs |'. 01.03.03-mandate-scope-delegated-authority.md:48 — '**The seed includes `administer`.** Any confirmed permanent member can therefore alter another member's mandate, invite, and remove.' (no ceiling qualifier). 01.04.01-partnership-terms-decision-rules.md:36 — 'every permanent member can do anything for the band up to USD 1,000, including changing what the others can do and removing them; above that it goes to whoever created the band' (permission changes INSIDE the ceiling). 01.01.02-artist-names-aliases-projects.md:92 (E-28 copy) — 'Everyone here will also be able to act for the band — book, sign, spend, settle — up to $1,000 each, and change each other's permissions.' (permission changes OUTSIDE the ceiling). 01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md:173 (D-14) — 'a multi-member band always retains confirmed permanent members holding the full activity set, so it is never unadministrable for acts below the ceiling' (implies administer acts are ceiling-bounded and some exceed it). 01.04.01-partnership-terms-decision-rules.md:89 (D-05) — '**The governance disclosure and the mandate surface must state the same authority in the same words**'. No open question covers this: 01.03.03 Q-03 asks whether the ceiling should become band-agreed, Q-04 asks the representation-edge default; neither addresses unvalued acts.
findings.failureScenario: A four-piece band forms with nothing configured. The drummer, a confirmed permanent member, opens the band's people surface and removes the guitarist and revokes their mandate. Implementer A treats `administer` as unvalued and therefore always within the USD 1,000 ceiling, so the removal succeeds silently. Implementer B treats an unvalued act as unbounded and therefore above any ceiling, so it escalates to the band's creator for approval. The same band, the same act, and the two builds differ on who may eject a member — the single most consequential act in the sub-domain — and the E-28 and 01.04.01 disclosure copy each supports a different one.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether an unclaimed party's public page names the human who created it and attested its credits.
findings.claim: 01.06.02 D-02 and 01.06.01's provenance table forbid publishing attester identity to any viewer at any tier, while 01.05.01 D-03, 01.06.01's own unclaimed-page edge case and States row, and 01.01.01's Unowned state all require the creating attester to be named on that same public page. Neither side carries a marker or an exception.
findings.evidence: 01.06.02-credit-backed-portfolio.md:63 — '| **Attester identity** | ❌ **Never, at any tier, to any viewer including authenticated professionals** | `02.01.02` DT-04 |', restated at :211 (D-02) 'Evidence class and count publish; attester identity never does — at any tier, to any viewer.' 01.06.01-profile-page-composition.md:41 — '**Attested** | ... The graph holds who; **the page never publishes the attester's identity — at any tier, to any viewer** (01.06.02 D-02)'. Against that: 01.05.01-shadow-party-creation-invitation.md:44 — '| **Creator** | Yes | The authenticated party that named it. Immutable. **Never hidden from a viewer of the shadow page.** |', and :204 (D-03) 'Every shadow party records its creator, immutably and visibly'. 01.06.01-profile-page-composition.md:109 — 'Even the Header is creator-asserted (a Producer typed "Sam — horn"), marked with its creator (01.05.01 D-03) | "Added by Sam Reeves" on the header.' 01.01.01-person-record-role-facets.md:146 (Unowned state) — 'Other-asserted facets render with their attester named ("credited as a performer by Sam Reeves").' 01.01.01-person-record-role-facets.md:123 — 'The shadow record carries **other-asserted** facets ... marked as other-asserted with the attester named.'
findings.failureScenario: A Producer credits a horn player at a session, creating a shadow party. A stranger opens that unclaimed page. Implementer A follows 01.06.02 D-02 and renders 'Confirmed by 1 person who was there' with no name — which also removes the accountability mechanism 01.05.01 DT-02 relies on to make an unauthenticated creation surface survivable, and removes the 'Added by Sam Reeves' header 01.06.01 specifies. Implementer B follows 01.05.01 D-03 and prints 'Added by Sam Reeves' plus 'credited as a performer by Sam Reeves' — publishing exactly the attester identity 01.06.02 DT-05 calls 'the most dangerous sentence in this file' on privacy and moat grounds. The two builds differ on whether the platform publicly discloses who vouched for whom, on the highest-traffic unauthenticated surface in the product.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether reclassifying a private seller to trader retroactively publishes their real name and geographic address on listings that were already live.
findings.claim: The domain CX file names this as unmodelled and consequential and defers it to a stage the tree elsewhere records as already completed, with no owner. No open question in 01.08 or 01.01.04 picks it up: 01.08 Q-01 covers the disposition on a detection trip (prompt / reclassify / block), and Q-02 covers what the disclosure says, not whether it applies backwards.
findings.evidence: identity-profiles-organizations-cx.md:187 (CX-08 §5) — '**State transition conflict**: A private seller reclassified to trader with live listings — do their existing listings retroactively publish their address? Unmodelled and consequential. `[PENDING — /ideate-validate]`'. Echoed at :325 (CX-17 §5) — 'A trader reclassification with live listings — the retroactive-publication race is CX-08 §5, `[PENDING — /ideate-validate]`.' The target stage has run: 01.02.01-organization-types-attributes.md:164 — '**Re-targeted 2026-07-23**: drilling has run and the owning file now carries it', and 01.02.02-organization-creation-lifecycle.md:264 — '`/ideate-validate` has already run without taking it.' 01.08-trader-status-classification.md:90 (D-05) requires the address disclosure be made 'before listing, prominently' — a rule with no defined behaviour for listings that predate the classification.
findings.failureScenario: A musician lists eight pedals over four months as a private seller. Detection trips and reclassifies them to trader. Implementer A applies D-05 literally — the disclosure is a pre-listing gate — so the eight live listings keep running with no trader details, leaving the platform publishing eight non-compliant listings. Implementer B applies the classification to the party and re-renders every listing, so the seller's home address appears publicly on eight listings without the blocking disclosure D-05 says they must see first. One build is a compliance breach, the other is an unconsented home-address publication.

findings.forcedInvention: What an org does when a counterparty refuses to resolve an obligation that blocks a type removal.
findings.claim: 01.02.03 specifies type removal as a hard block on live obligations. 01.02.02 explicitly identifies that this reproduces the counterparty-hostage failure its own DT-07 rejected for closure, and says the case 'wants the same `closing`-shaped intent state' — but 01.02.03 was not amended and carries no open question covering it, so the identified defect is neither fixed nor tracked.
findings.evidence: 01.02.03-organization-type-transitions.md:45 — '| Type removed while its data is live (removing `venue` with shows booked) | Blocked, same rule as closure (01.02.02) | "You have upcoming shows as a venue. Resolve them before removing this capability." |'. 01.02.02-organization-creation-lifecycle.md:225 — '**Two escalations**: ... (b) that file's "type removed while its data is live ⇒ blocked" carries DT-07's hostage bug and wants the same `closing`-shaped intent state.' 01.02.02-organization-creation-lifecycle.md:207 (DT-07) — 'Closure blocked must not mean closure denied. The `closing` intent state (D-09) resolves it.' 01.02.03's Open Questions are only Q-01 (band+label as two legal entities) and Q-02 (reputation across types); neither touches this.
findings.failureScenario: A studio that added `venue` two years ago wants to stop hosting gigs. One promoter holds an unsettled balance from a show and will not sign off. Under 01.02.03 as written the `venue` type can never be removed, so the studio stays in venue search, keeps receiving booking enquiries it will not accept, and the promoter has an indefinite unilateral hold on the studio's capability set — the exact hostage state 01.02.02 D-09 built `closing` to prevent for the identical situation one level up.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether the capacity enum contains a `crew` value.
findings.claim: D-03 and the Behavior attribute table fix capacity as a closed four-value enum, and D-03 records that a fifth value was deliberately removed. The worked example in the Edge Cases table uses a value that is not in it.
findings.evidence: 01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md:162 (D-03) — '| D-03 | Capacity is on the edge (**permanent / touring / staff / honorary**), not on the person | `session` **removed** from the enum per D-05 ... |'. 01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md:34 — '| **Capacity periods** | permanent / touring / staff / honorary, each with its own date range | Versioned, not overwritten (D-10) |'. Against that, 01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md:82 — 'capacity is a list ("**crew** 2015–2017, staff 2017–2020, permanent 2020–")', with the scenario titled 'A member's capacity changes over time (roadie → sound engineer → member)'.
findings.failureScenario: An implementer builds the capacity enum from D-03 as {permanent, touring, staff, honorary} and then cannot represent the file's own canonical worked example, because the 2015–2017 roadie period has no admissible value. They either invent a fifth enum member (`crew`), silently coerce roadies to `staff` — which changes nothing for authority today but does change the lineup display the file says every band's own website separates — or reject the example. 01.03.03 D-09 keys the peer seed on capacity, so any invented value also needs a seeding rule nobody has written.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether a membership edge may hold two capacities at once, and if so how the peer seed resolves for a member who is simultaneously `permanent` (seeded with everything) and `staff` (seeded with nothing).
findings.claim: The Happy Path shows a single capacity period holding two capacities; D-10's worked example shows a strictly sequential single-valued list. The seed rule reads 'current capacity period is `permanent`', which presupposes exactly one current period, and D-09 gives `staff` zero authority — so a `permanent + staff` member has two contradictory seeds and no stated resolution.
findings.evidence: 01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md:63 — 'Their capacity period `permanent (2026–2028)` closes and `permanent + staff (2028–)` opens. Tenure is unbroken; the capacity history is a list.' 01.03.01-membership-records-lifecycle.md:82 — 'capacity is a list ("crew 2015–2017, staff 2017–2020, permanent 2020–")' — non-overlapping, single-valued. 01.03.03-mandate-scope-delegated-authority.md:40 — '| **Peer seed** (D-07) | Every **`confirmed`** membership edge whose **current capacity period is `permanent`** carries the **full seven-activity set** |'. 01.03.03-mandate-scope-delegated-authority.md:42 (D-09) — '`touring`, `staff` and `honorary` carry **presence with zero authority** until something is granted explicitly.'
findings.failureScenario: The band's drummer takes over front-of-house on the band's own shows and their edge becomes `permanent + staff` per the Happy Path. Implementer A models capacity as single-valued, cannot represent the state, and forces a choice — picking `staff` silently strips the drummer of all seven seeded activities including their acting context for the band. Implementer B models it as a set and unions the seeds, so `staff` is inert and nothing changes. Implementer C treats the zero-authority capacity as restrictive and intersects, again stripping the drummer. Three builds, three different answers to whether a founding member can still sign for their own band after taking on a crew role.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether an Operator can read a band's dissolution state and current name resolution.
findings.claim: The domain-level Role Matrix gives Operator no access to 01.04, and the accompanying note presents that as deliberate. Two of the four children grant Operator read-only access in both their sub-domain matrix row and their Role Lens, for reasons the children call operationally necessary.

findings.failureScenario: A downstream spec writer reads the domain Role Matrix (the pipeline's entry artefact for role scoping) and builds 01.04 with no Operator read path at all. The Fan column additionally aggregates permissively (👁️ at domain level over three ❌ children) while the Operator column aggregates restrictively, so the matrix has no consistent aggregation rule to fall back on.

findings.forcedInvention: How value ceilings combine when one human holds authority over the same party through two edges.
findings.claim: The rule that a person's authority is the union across edges but their ceiling is the maximum rather than the sum is stated only as an unconfirmed inline note with no owner, against a stage the tree records as completed. No open question in the sub-domain covers ceiling arithmetic across edges; 01.03.03 Q-04 covers only the unset representation ceiling.
findings.evidence: 01.03-membership-representation-mandate-cx.md:69 (CX-03 §3) — 'The union is deliberately not additive beyond the ceiling either — **the higher of two value ceilings applies, not their sum**. `[PENDING — Step 5: confirm]`'. 01.03.03-mandate-scope-delegated-authority.md:127 (Q-04) is scoped to 'What is a representation edge's value ceiling when none is set?' and says nothing about combination. 01.03-membership-representation-mandate-index.md:58 (Q-02) is scoped to per-type grants.
findings.failureScenario: A manager who is also a band member holds a membership edge seeded at USD 1,000 and a representation edge granted at USD 5,000. They accept a USD 5,500 offer. Implementer A takes the max (5,000) and blocks with escalation; implementer B sums (6,000) and allows it; implementer C evaluates per edge and blocks because neither edge alone covers it. The three builds differ on whether a USD 5,500 commitment binds the band.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether representation-term expiry produces any warning or notice, to whom, and when.
findings.claim: The sub-domain CX file names this as a gap, states it is currently unspecified, and defers it to a stage the tree records as completed, with no owner. 01.03.02's decision on expiry specifies the mechanical effect and no notification, and none of its five open questions covers it.
findings.evidence: 01.03-membership-representation-mandate-cx.md:81 (CX-04 §4) — '(4) **Gap**: expiry should warn ahead of time and on lapse; currently unspecified. Flagged for Step 5.' Context at :77 — 'An agent mid-negotiation on the last day of a term finds their context gone, with a live deal in it.' 01.03.02-representation-roster-relationships.md:91 (D-04) — 'Expiry removes the acting context automatically | Falls out of 01.01.03 D-01's derivation; no revocation sweep needed' — no notice. 01.03.02's Q-01..Q-05 cover commission tails, on-platform signing, the domain vocabulary, the overlap key, and the untyped edge attributes; none covers expiry notification. 01.03.02-representation-roster-relationships.md:45 shows the consequence untreated — 'An agent books a show after the term expired | Cannot — the acting context is gone ... | Context absent; deep link offers nothing'.
findings.failureScenario: An agent's two-year term lapses at midnight while they are mid-advance on a festival slot. Their acting context vanishes with no prior warning and no notice on lapse; the venue's counterparty simply stops replying. Implementer A ships silence (D-04 as written), implementer B invents a 30-day warning, implementer C notifies only on lapse. 01.01.03's own rule that a context appearing announces itself once ('New mandate granted ... **announces itself once**') has no stated mirror for disappearance.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether an attester whose own party is under contest still counts toward a claimant's Tier C threshold.
findings.claim: The sub-domain CX file records this as unspecified on an ownerless `[PENDING — Step 5]` marker against a completed stage. 01.05.02 specifies the independence test and the Tier B/C thresholds in full but never conditions them on the attester's own standing, and 01.05.01's nearest rule adjusts only the attester's dispatch tier, not their evidentiary weight.
findings.evidence: 01.05-profile-claiming-verification-cx.md:93 (CX-04 §5) — 'An attester's own party being contested while they act as a witness — **their evidentiary weight during that period is unspecified**. `[PENDING — Step 5]`'. 01.05.02-claim-initiation-proof-methods.md:54 defines independence only as co-membership, mandate relationship or shared session: '**Independence** ... means two attesters who are *not*: co-members of the same organisation, in a mandate relationship with each other (01.03), or attesting from the same session/project.' 01.05.01-shadow-party-creation-invitation.md:138 covers only dispatch — 'Creator's own party is suspended or contested while their shadows are live | The shadows stand ... The creator's *tier* drops to 0 for the duration'. Neither 01.05.02's Q-01/Q-02/Q-03 nor 01.05.03's Q-01..Q-06 covers it.
findings.failureScenario: Two people contest the same venue page. The challenger's Tier C evidence is two confirmations, one of them from a Producer whose own person party is simultaneously under contest by a third party. Implementer A counts it and the challenger reaches full-control threshold; implementer B discounts it and the challenger stays provisional; implementer C freezes. The same evidence yields control, provisional control, or a frozen party depending on an unwritten rule.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether counterparties holding an active legal-identity disclosure are told when the subject's legal name changes.
findings.claim: The sub-domain CX file leaves this on an ownerless inline marker against a completed stage. 01.01.04's Edge Cases specify what happens to the record and to historic contracts but not whether the parties currently holding the disclosure are notified, and neither of its two open questions covers it.
findings.evidence: 01.01-person-identity-roles-cx.md:74 (CX-03 §4) — '**Notification fan-out**: A legal name change notifies nobody publicly. Counterparties with an active disclosure `[PENDING — Step 5: do they get told?]`.' 01.01.04-legal-identity-vs-public-identity.md:46 — 'User changes their legal name ... New legal name applies going forward. Historic contracts keep the name that was true when signed ... The old name is **not** shown to anyone new' — silent on existing disclosure holders. 01.01.04's Q-01 (stalking posture) and Q-02 (pseudonymous split sheets) do not cover it. 01.01.04-legal-identity-vs-public-identity.md:58 makes the disclosure ledger a first-class object — 'Populated | Legal identity captured | A disclosure ledger: who has been shown it, for what, when' — so the recipient set is known and the choice is a real one.
findings.failureScenario: A trans artist changes their legal name after signing three split sheets. Implementer A pushes an update to the three counterparties holding the disclosure, which discloses the transition to three people who did not need to know. Implementer B says nothing, so a co-signatory later files a registration under a legal name the platform knows is stale. Both are defensible from the text and they are opposite products for the exact user 01.01.04 exists to protect.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether deleting an empty alias returns its handle to the pool.
findings.claim: D-01 permits deleting a zero-everything alias and DT-08's stated rationale is that forced retirement 'burns a handle for nothing' — implying release. D-09 states without qualification that old handles are never re-issued. Q-05 tracks only the dormant/abandoned case, not the explicit-delete case, so neither reading is marked.
findings.evidence: 01.01.02-artist-names-aliases-projects.md:149 (D-01) — 'Retirement, not deletion — **except** an alias with zero credits, releases, followers, posts and identifiers, which is deletable'. 01.01.02-artist-names-aliases-projects.md:122 (DT-08) — 'Forcing permanent retirement on a typo litters the settings surface forever **and burns a handle for nothing**.' Against that, 01.01.02-artist-names-aliases-projects.md:157 (D-09) — '**Old handles resolve permanently and are never re-issued.** Handle changes: 2 per alias per rolling 12 months.' Q-05 at :169 is scoped elsewhere — '**Is a dormant handle ever reclaimable?** ... a user who abandons `wejamm.in/nova` in 2027 holds it against every later Nova forever' — dormancy, not deletion. E-15 at :79 uses release language for the failure case only: 'A failure never leaves a handle reserved against an alias that does not exist — that would burn the namespace invisibly.'
findings.failureScenario: A user creates `wejamm.in/nova` by typo, deletes it thirty seconds later with nothing attached, then a different artist tries to register `nova`. Implementer A applies D-09 and refuses forever, permanently burning a handle for a typo — the outcome DT-08 says the deletion exception exists to prevent. Implementer B releases it, so `wejamm.in/nova` is now re-issuable, and the assumption DT-09 relies on ('if `wejamm.in/old-name` is re-issuable, whoever takes it inherits every link the artist ever printed') acquires an exception nobody wrote a bound for.

findings.forcedInvention: Whether an EPK may render non-public content (rates, contact routes) behind a forwardable no-auth link.
findings.claim: D-06 justifies the absence of an access gate on the premise that the per-recipient link only wraps public content. The same file's Behavior lists rates among the assembled material and its Edge Cases concede the kit 'may contain rates and contact routes not meant for the world'. Both cannot hold; Q-03 tracks a possible remedy (expiry/revocation) but not the premise, and the edge case points the reader at Q-02, which is about PDF export.
findings.evidence: 01.06.03-epk-generation-sharing.md:99 (D-06) — '| D-06 | Per-recipient link is a tracking wrapper over **public content**, not an access gate | Forwarding to a decision-making room must work for strangers with no account (D-03) |'. Against that: 01.06.03-epk-generation-sharing.md:52 — '| Link is shared publicly | An EPK **may contain rates and contact routes not meant for the world** | Needs expiry/revocation. See Q-02 |'; :17 — 'Producer | Full | Generates a client-facing kit: discography, room, **rates**, turnaround, testimonials'; :51 — 'The per-recipient link is a *tracking wrapper over public content*, not an access gate, so a forward opens fine for a stranger with no account.' Q-03 at :107 asks only 'Do share links expire or get revoked'; Q-02 at :106 is the PDF-export question the edge case mis-cites.
findings.failureScenario: A producer generates a client kit with their day rate and mobile number and sends it to one label A&R. Implementer A takes D-06 literally, renders only content already public on the profile, and silently drops the rates — the kit no longer makes the pitch it was generated for. Implementer B renders the rates behind the no-auth wrapper, and the A&R forwards it to a group thread; the producer's rate card and mobile number are now permanently public with no revocation path, on a link D-06 declares needs no gate.

findings.forcedInvention: Which maturity status each child has actually reached.
findings.claim: The domain index's Children table and its own Status header disagree with the Status headers of the files they describe, in both directions: three leaf features are listed one grade below their own headers, and all six sub-domain rows are listed at `[BREADTH]` while their children are `[DEEP]`.
findings.evidence: identity-profiles-organizations-index.md:38-40 — '| 01.07 | ... | `[SURFACE]` |', '| 01.08 | ... | `[SURFACE]` |', '| 01.09 | ... | `[SURFACE]` |'. Against that: 01.07-professional-credential-verification.md:5 — '> **Status**: [PARTIAL]'; 01.08-trader-status-classification.md:5 — '> **Status**: [PARTIAL]'; 01.09-party-identifier-resolution.md:5 — '> **Status**: [PARTIAL]'. Likewise identity-profiles-organizations-index.md:32-37 lists all six sub-domains `[BREADTH]`, while 01.01-person-identity-roles-index.md:18-20 lists three of its four children `[DEEP]` and 01.06-portfolio-media-epk-index.md:20-21 lists two of three `[DEEP]`. The domain index's own header (:5) reads '> **Status**: [BREADTH]' while its CX file (identity-profiles-organizations-cx.md:5) reads '> **Status**: [DEEP]'.
findings.failureScenario: A remediation or planning stage that gates on maturity — deciding which nodes still need a deepening pass, or which are safe to decompose — reads the domain index as the pipeline key file, sees six `[BREADTH]` sub-domains and four `[SURFACE]` features, and schedules deepening work on 22 files that are already `[DEEP]` or `[PARTIAL]`, or conversely treats the domain as too immature to decompose when its content carries ratified DQ-02 and DQ-R2-01 decisions.
